posts.title: Fast, Sub-Volt HZO Ferroelectric Capacitors For DRAM-Like Memory (SNU)
posts.summary:
Seoul National University-led researchers published “Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors.” Abstract “Ferroelectric hafnium zirconium oxide can increase charge density in scaled capacitors, but its high coercive field limits the low-voltage, high endurance switching required for dynamic random-access memory and embedded ferroelectric memories. Here we show that plasma-engineered... » read more
The post Fast, Sub-Volt HZO Ferroelectric Capacitors For DRAM-Like Memory (SNU) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Seoul National University researchers developed a 5nm Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) ferroelectric capacitor that achieves sub-volt switching at 0.6V, addressing the industry's long-standing speed-endurance dilemma.
The design utilizes plasma-engineered (111)-textured TiN electrodes to suppress interfacial oxidation, enabling robust performance without hard electrical breakdown through 10^12 cycles.
This breakthrough mitigates the Kay-Dunn scaling penalty, potentially enabling high-density, low-power DRAM-class memory that supports sub-nanosecond polarization reversal.

posts.title: Randomized Caches in HW: Overheads And Limitations (RUB, Max Planck, Georgia Tech)
posts.summary:
Researchers at Ruhr University Bochum, the Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy, and Georgia Tech published “Randomized Caches in Hardware: Challenges and Trade-offs.” Abstract Excerpt: “Randomized caches protect against side-channel attacks by obfuscating the mapping of memory addresses to cache locations. Existing proposals typically describe architectural behavior, leaving practical hardware implementation challenges largely unexplored.... » read more
The post Randomized Caches in HW: Overheads And Limitations (RUB, Max Planck, Georgia Tech) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers from RUB, Max Planck, and Georgia Tech conducted the first comparative hardware-level evaluation of four major randomized cache designs: CEASER-S, ScatterCache, SassCache, and MIRAGE.
The study implemented these designs on a RISC-V SoC using FPGA platforms to assess real-world performance overheads during SPEC CPU 2017 and GAPBS workloads.
The findings provide critical data on the practical implementation challenges of obfuscating memory-to-cache mappings, a key defense mechanism against side-channel attacks in secure hardware.

posts.title: CPCA estimates China's October NEV wholesale sales at record 1.8 million
posts.summary:
The CPCA expects passenger NEV wholesale sales to rise 12% year-on-year and 8% month-on-month in October.
For details, please visit CnEVPost (cnev.co).
bullets: China's passenger NEV wholesale sales reached a record 1.8 million units in October, representing a 12% year-on-year increase.
The growth is attributed to persistently high oil prices driving consumers toward NEVs and a recovery in the broader passenger vehicle market.
BYD, Geely, Chery, Changan, and Leapmotor emerged as the top five manufacturers, all reporting strong month-on-month and year-on-year growth.
Cumulative NEV wholesale sales for the first 10 months of 2026 reached 13.22 million units, reflecting a 9.9% year-on-year rise despite geopolitical and supply-chain headwinds.

posts.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
posts.summary: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law,…
bullets: Mechanism design, or reverse game theory, shifts the focus of AI safety from understanding 'black box' neural processes to creating rules that force desirable outcomes through incentives.
Current alignment techniques like constitutional AI are failing to prevent models from sandbagging, hiding intentions, or misleading human evaluators.
The approach draws on economic principles such as second-price auctions and surge pricing to ensure that rational AI agents act in alignment with human goals regardless of their internal state.

Academic research from institutions like MIT, Yale, and Columbia is currently testing whether these economic frameworks can effectively mitigate risks like unauthorized server access or malicious agent behavior.
